GBR.story:
Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958. Two police investigations in his lifetime produced no charges, Surrey Police dropped an inquiry in 2007–09, and in December 2011 the BBC shelved a report about him by its own Newsnight programme. In October 2012 London's Metropolitan Police opened Operation Yewtree, and in 2013 it recorded 214 crimes by him. Later inquiries found victims aged 5 to 75 in hospitals of the state health service.

In Rotherham, children's-home managers and youth workers reported the sexual exploitation of children from the early-to-mid 1990s, and the researcher Angie Heal warned officials from 2002 to 2007. A rape reported in 2001 ended with the suspect released without charge, and action against the abusers began only in 2010. An independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited in the town between 1997 and 2013, and called the failures of the council and the police 'blatant'. The National Crime Agency, the national agency for serious crime, then took over the case; it has identified about 1,150 potential victims, and 39 people have been convicted. In Oxfordshire a review in 2015 found that police did not believe the girls and treated them as if they had chosen their situation.

Medomsley Detention Centre in County Durham held young male offenders from 1961 to 1988. Neville Husband, the officer who ran its kitchens, was convicted of sexual offences in 2003 and 2005, and eight former staff were jailed. In November 2025 the Prisons and Probation Ombudsman, the independent investigator of complaints about prisons, found that what the Prison Service, the police and the Home Office knew of the abuse had been 'ignored and dismissed'.

From June 2026 people in England and Wales who were abused as children can sue however long ago the abuse happened, unless the defendant shows a fair trial is impossible. The National Crime Agency is now investigating allegations that former South Yorkshire Police officers abused children, and no finding has yet been made.

KEN.story:
In December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs published a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 percent of girls aged 12 to 18 living there were involved in casual sex work, and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex. Kenyans made up 38 percent of the buyers, and tourists from Italy, Germany and Switzerland 44 percent. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and said the police and local communities had failed to enforce the law.

The trade continued and moved. The 2025 US State Department trafficking report cites a 2023 study by a non-governmental organisation estimating that more than 2,000 children were sold for sex in Kilifi and Kwale counties, and says the abuse there is moving from hotels into private villas and holiday homes. The report also describes rings bringing underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and notes concerns that officials take part, with no action reported against any of them.

Babies and young children were also bought and sold in Nairobi. In 2020 a year-long BBC investigation found children taken from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350 to £550, A clinical social worker at Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital, a government hospital, sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings. The BBC said he appeared to keep his job.

Since the 2006 study no Kenyan government inquiry appears in the records gathered for this map, and what is known has come from foreign governments, charities and journalists. The most recent describe children still sold for sex on the coast.
removed: Paragraph on abuse at Nyumbani children's home, Nairobi (USAID 2021 finding, co-founder's resignation)

CHE.story:
Mainly from 1930 to 1981, Swiss cantonal and municipal authorities sent more than 60,000 people to about 650 institutions without any court order, a practice known as administrative detention. They included the Verdingkinder, children placed with farmers as indentured labourers. Those held were abused physically, psychologically and sexually.

The Swiss government apologised in 2010. A 2016 law gave victims of these compulsory measures a "solidarity contribution" of CHF 25,000, and in 2019 an independent expert commission published its final report.

From the 1970s, Swiss families adopted children from abroad, including 1,111 from South Korea between 1968 and 1997 and others from Sri Lanka, India and Tibet. Swiss authorities realised that many children had been wrongly presented as orphans, and that placements were driven by money and linked to organised child trafficking. Decisions often rested on incomplete or falsified documents. After pressure from adoptees' groups such as Back to the Roots, parliament commissioned a study in 2018. The Federal Council, the Swiss government, acknowledged the authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

In 2023 historians at the University of Zurich, in a study paid for by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders, documented 1,002 cases of sexual abuse in the Catholic Church since 1950, with 510 accused people and 921 victims. Of the documents, 74 percent concerned minors, and about 30 percent of cases took place in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers found that church law was hardly ever applied and that many cases were kept secret.

The state has apologised to and paid victims of the forced placements, and the government has proposed ending intercountry adoption. The church researchers said the cases they found were only a small part of the total, so the full number of children abused in the church is not known.

USA.story:
In 1974 the bishop of the Diocese of Lafayette, in Louisiana, made Fr Gilbert Gauthe a Boy Scout chaplain despite allegations that he had abused altar boys. In 1976 Gauthe was sent for therapy and then returned to work. He later admitted abusing 37 children, and in 1985 he pleaded guilty and was sentenced to 20 years. His was the first widely publicised prosecution of a priest for abuse in the United States.

Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997. The FBI was told in July 2015 but did not act, and the Justice Department's internal watchdog found that at least 70 more athletes were abused between the reports to the FBI and his arrest. By his final hearing, 265 victims had been identified.

In 2005 Palm Beach police in Florida investigated the financier Jeffrey Epstein and identified about 35 girls, but a state grand jury, a panel of citizens that decides on charges, returned only a single count of soliciting prostitution. In 2007 the federal prosecutor's office under Alexander Acosta agreed not to bring federal charges against Epstein and several suspected co-conspirators and kept the agreement from the victims. Epstein served 13 months of an 18-month state sentence.

When states proposed lengthening the legal deadlines for suing over childhood abuse, Catholic organisations, insurers and the Scouts lobbied against the changes. At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts of America and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy facing abuse claims.

No national inquiry into abuse in American institutions has been held; the investigations have been by state attorneys general and grand juries, or commissioned by the church.
removed: Jerry Sandusky / Penn State sentences (1998 and 2001 reports, 2012 conviction, 2017 convictions of university officials)

ZAF.story:
In 1979 Fettes College, a school in Edinburgh, dismissed the teacher Iain Wares but gave him a glowing reference. He went on to teach in South Africa, where he later abused children; South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025. Fr Georg Kerkhoff, a German priest with abuse cases pending at home, worked in South Africa and was tried there for abusing boys at a 2008 camp before being extradited and jailed in Germany in 2015.

The British barrister John Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, after a 1982 internal report of the Iwerne Trust, the evangelical charity he had chaired, described how he beat boys he met at its camps. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001. The Makin Review, published in England in 2024, found it highly likely that he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018. He was never charged anywhere.

In June 2026 the South African Human Rights Commission described sexual violence in schools as systemic. It recorded 826 complaints of sexual misconduct made between 2021 and 2025 to the South African Council for Educators, the body that registers teachers. It found that a teacher struck off by the council is not automatically added to the register of people barred from working with children, and that 10,748 convicted offenders had not been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.

The 2025 US State Department trafficking report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and sell them for sex in Gauteng and Western Cape, that brothel owners use drugs to control them, that some parents sell their own children, and that low-level corruption and complicity among officials continued.

Because of the gaps the commission found, teachers removed for sexual misconduct and convicted sex offenders may be missing from the registers meant to keep them away from South African children.

DOM.story:
In 2008 the Vatican sent the Polish archbishop Józef Wesołowski to the Dominican Republic as its nuncio, the Vatican's ambassador. In August 2013, amid allegations that he was abusing minors, the Vatican recalled him to Rome, and in September Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation. Once he was in the Vatican he was out of reach of Dominican courts, and the Vatican later told Polish prosecutors that its law did not allow him to be extradited. A church tribunal found him guilty and he was dismissed from the priesthood in 2014. In 2015 a Vatican prosecutor charged him with abusing children in the Dominican Republic between 2008 and 2013 and with possessing abuse images, but he was found dead in August 2015, before the trial.

A Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, Fr Wojciech Gil, was suspended in May 2013 and returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic. Polish police arrested him in 2014 using Dominican evidence, and in 2015 a Polish court sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic and two in Poland.

Children are also sold for sex to visitors in the Dominican Republic's tourist towns. In April 2015 Dominican authorities, working with US Homeland Security Investigations, freed 29 victims, 20 of them aged 14 to 17, in the north-coast town of Sosúa and arrested seven Dominican nationals. The US State Department's 2025 report says teenage girls are often exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and charities link the growing number of child victims to weak regulation of tourism.

The cases against the two clergymen were decided in Poland and the Vatican, not in the country where the children lived. Exploitation of children in tourist areas continues.
removed: Sentence on US men prosecuted at home for abusing children on the north coast (Troy Brimm, Puerto Plata)

VNM.story:
From 1994 to 2014 the United States alone issued 7,498 immigrant visas to children adopted from Hanoi, with a peak of 828 in 2007.

In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi reported that the number of babies recorded as abandoned had risen 17-fold or more at orphanages in seven provinces. Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the United States when it expired that September. In 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and doctors and nurses at village clinics, for abuse of power. They were accused of asking poor families for their infants and falsifying documents to say the babies had been abandoned, and 266 babies were sent abroad for adoption between 2005 and 2008. Vietnam still sent 14,039 children abroad between 2003 and 2022, and in Belgium the Flemish government later stopped adoptions from Vietnam.

Foreigners also came to Vietnam to abuse children. In 2007 an Australian charity found 80 commercial cases of child exploitation by foreigners in Sa Pa, and the same year Vietnam set up a unit in the Ministry of Public Security to investigate child sex tourism. In 2006 a Vietnamese court had convicted the British singer Paul Gadd, known as Gary Glitter, of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11.

Vietnamese children are also trafficked out of the country. The 2025 US State Department report on trafficking says traffickers in border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages, and Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024. In Britain, 416 Vietnamese children were referred as potential victims of modern slavery that year, and Vietnamese children and adults there are exploited on cannabis farms and in nail salons.

Adoption from Vietnam has been cut back after the fraud cases. Vietnamese girls continue to be trafficked to China, and Vietnamese children to Britain.

BOL.story:
In 1964 the Spanish Jesuit priest Alfonso Pedrajas abused a child in Lima, Peru, and then settled in Bolivia, where he worked in Jesuit schools. In 1978 he confessed to a superior, who covered it up. In a diary published by the Spanish newspaper El País in 2023, Pedrajas, who died in 2009, wrote that he had abused at least 85 minors between 1972 and 2000. In May 2023 prosecutors seized internal Jesuit documents in La Paz and Cochabamba. On 2 September 2025 a Bolivian court sentenced Marcos Recolons and Ramón Alaix, former provincials, or heads of the Jesuits in Bolivia, to one year in prison each for knowing of allegations against Pedrajas and not reporting them. Sentences under three years are normally commuted in Bolivia, meaning replaced by a lighter penalty. Prosecutors said they would pursue other priests named at the trial.

In its 2025 report on trafficking, the US State Department said foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni. It said the production of abuse material for sale online was rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz, and that Bolivian women and girls were exploited in sex trafficking in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru.

The Jesuit superiors were convicted for failing to report, and prosecutors have said more priests may be charged. The abuse by foreign visitors and the abuse filmed for sale online are known mainly from a US government report.
removed: Paragraph on the Manitoba Mennonite Colony 'ghost rapes' (2005–2009, 2011 convictions)

AUT.story:
In September 1995 Cardinal Hans Hermann Groër, the Archbishop of Vienna, stepped down after former pupils accused him of sexual abuse. In 1998 the Austrian bishops said they considered the allegations well founded.

In spring 2010 the bishops set up the Independent Victims' Protection Commission, chaired by Waltraud Klasnic, to pay victims of church abuse. By 31 August 2021 payments had been approved in 2,550 cases, about €33 million in total.

Inquiries into homes run by cities and states followed. In 2013 a commission on the city's Wilhelminenberg home found that girls as young as about six had been raped and sexually exploited there by caregivers and outside men, and that city staff and politicians who knew of it in the 1960s did not act. From 2010 the city paid the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring to handle claims, and by 2019 it had paid 42.13 million euros to victims. In 2015 a University of Innsbruck study for the states of Tyrol and Vorarlberg found that their homes kept children isolated and dependent on staff, a system that produced and tolerated sexualised violence until the 1980s.

In October 2025, after reporting by the magazine Falter, the Austrian branch of the SOS Children's Villages charity said there were credible allegations that its founder, Hermann Gmeiner, who died in 1986, had abused eight boys between the 1950s and 1980s. Victims had come forward from 2013 and been compensated, but the charity had not made this public. Prosecutors in three cities opened investigations, and in 2026 a reform commission chaired by the former Supreme Court president Irmgard Griss examined the lack of outside oversight of the villages.

Most of the abuse found in Austria took place in church, city and state homes between 1945 and the 1990s, and has mainly led to compensation payments. The allegations against Gmeiner, kept inside the charity for years, are still under investigation.
removed: Sentence on Kremsmünster Abbey boarding school abuse and the 2013 sentence of its former boarding director

MLT.story:
In 1991 the Catholic bishops of Malta set up a Response Team, chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, to deal with complaints of abuse by clergy. In April 2010 the Maltese Curia, the church's central administration, said the team had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 were still open, four priests had been found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died.

Children from Malta were also sent abroad. Under child migration schemes, British and Maltese children were sent to institutions in Australia, among them homes run by the Christian Brothers, a Catholic religious order, at Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf and Tardun in Western Australia. In August 2001 a committee of the Australian Senate reported that of 207 former child migrants who wrote to it, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

The figures on abuse by clergy in Malta come from the church's own Response Team. The abuse of Maltese child migrants was examined in Australia, together with that of British children.
